content.text:
The Child Whose Feet Freeze at the Water's Edge

The other kids splash around happily, but your child alone hugs a float at the water's edge and freezes. Even touching a toe makes their body flinch, and though they watch with envious eyes, they can't go in.

Fear of water is a very common feeling. Rushing them with "It's fine, get in quick" only makes the water scarier. What a child needs isn't a push, but a steady hand.

Curious about the fear-of-water story? We look at the lesson of the story through pictures. Meet the key scenes of the fear-of-water story too. Read it together with your child and talk it over. We've gathered all kinds of stories about "29. Let Your Body Go Loose, and Float!"—fear of swimming, overcoming water fear, toddler water-play safety, and more.

content.alt: 29. Let Your Body Go Loose, and Float! - Fear is overcome little by little
content.text:
Fear Is Overcome Little by Little

Fear can't be erased all at once. Forcing a child in only imprints it more deeply. Instead, stacking up very small successes one by one lets the fear fade naturally.

Dipping in a toe, going in up to the knee—each one is a big challenge for a child. When you respect and praise these little steps at the child's own pace, they learn how to find courage on their own.

content.alt: 29. Let Your Body Go Loose, and Float! - Bori and Dad's step-by-step water play
content.text:
Bori and Dad's Step-by-Step Water Play

In the story Let Your Body Go Loose, and Float!, Bori is scared of the water and sits back at the edge. Hori's dad comes over and whispers, "You don't have to do it all at once. Just a little toe."

When Bori dips in a toe, the water tickles—cooler and more fun than expected. Holding Dad's hand, one step, two steps. At last, resting on the float and letting the body go loose, Bori bobs up and floats. "I'm floating!"

3 Ways to Make Friends With Water, From Tangobook

The heart of this story is three steps that are easy for a child to follow. One, start little by little from the toes! Two, hold a grown-up's hand tight! Three, let your body go loose and float!

Tangobook's story repeats these steps like a refrain, helping your child recall them naturally when facing water play. Through Bori's challenge, your child feels that even when it's scary, doing a little at a time makes it fun.

content.text:
Preparing for Happy Water Play at Home

Before heading out to play in the water, read this story together and practice "little by little from the toes!" in advance. Small games of getting friendly with water in the bathtub or at the sink help too.

During real water play, always stay within reach of a grown-up's hand, and praise every little toe-dip in a big way. When you respect the child's pace instead of rushing, water becomes not a scary place but a joyful one.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I help a child who's scared of the water?

A. Rather than forcing them in, show them like play that when the body goes loose, it floats. Getting friendly with water little by little, starting from the feet, gradually shrinks the fear.

Q. Will a fear-of-water story help?

A. Watching the hero in the story become friends with water gives your child courage too. A fear-of-water story naturally teaches that water isn't only something to fear.

Q. My child fears water—should I still start swimming?

A. It's important to first get friendly with water at the child's pace and not rush. Once they build up joyful experiences in the water, they'll want to try more on their own.
